title: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This tendency to revolution—“circumvolution,” as Darwin calls it, “revolving nutation,” as Sachs puts it—is very closely comparable to the process by which an antelope’s horn (such as the koodoo’s) grows into its spiral or rather helicoid form; and it is simply due, in like manner, to inequalities in the rate of growth on different sides of the growing stem.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Torsion in climbing plants”. Scope: twining climbing plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern kinematics makes the mechanism directly testable, and some public time-lapse studies can address it. Existing coverage is unlikely to resolve the full scope of twining plants.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Analyze time-lapse stem growth to estimate side-specific elongation and test whether the moving growth asymmetry predicts circumvolution direction, phase and curvature. Correct temporal prediction supports the mechanism; twining without differential growth or phase mismatch refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Repository coverage of side-specific elongation is uncertain.

Twining species and growth conditions are heterogeneous.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Unequal flank growth is a measurable alternative to uniform elongation, and classic and later experiments report it for particular twiners. Those measurements are not assembled as a public dataset a team could download and reanalyze, and they rarely span the diversity of climbing stems. The comparison with horn growth is an analogy; the plant data that exist can test local differential growth in a few species only.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: During circumnutation, compare epidermal or cortical extension rates on opposite flanks along the elongating stem. The claim is supported if the revolving bend is accompanied by a rotating excess of growth on the convex side over a long zone of the stem; it is weakened if the stem revolves while flank growth rates remain equal.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Kinematic and local-strain measurements of twining stems are scattered in papers rather than held in one open repository.

Most series cover one or two model climbers, not twining plants as a class.
